case_study_insert.main_stem: Minegate Minerals (MNG) is a private limited company in the industrial minerals sector, employing a workforce of 50 at its silica-sand purification plant. Founded in 2015 by Tomas Minegate, the business supplies low-iron silica sand to solar-glass makers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MNG plans to invest $600,000 in a magnetic-separation plant to remove iron impurities, financed by a $250,000 bank overdraft facility and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.00, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. MNG faces two problems: a skills gap in operating the new separators and an impurity-related rejection rate of 5.4%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The purification line processed 18,750 units last quarter, of which 5.4% were rejected for excess iron, down from 7.9% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 29 to 12 per month. Average order lead time is 6.3 days. A survey of 540 solar-glass buyers found that 59% would pay up to $0.70 more for low-iron sand, and 71% require purity certificates. A skills audit shows 12 of the 50 operators lack experience with magnetic separators and have had no on-the-job training on the separators; off-the-job external courses cost $1,250 per employee. The operations manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Minegate Minerals for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Manufacturing Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has increased the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.10%, raising the cost of short-term borrowing such as bank overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.10 to $14.00 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage costs at the plant. (3) Energy and separation-medium input costs have risen 12.8% year-on-year, while industrial-minerals inflation is 8.3% and solar-panel installation grew 4.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: MNG is using a $250,000 bank overdraft facility for part of its $600,000 separation plant. Explain two advantages for MNG of using retained profit for the $350,000 portion instead of a larger overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge, whereas a bigger overdraft would add to the interest payable of $26,000 already shown in Appendix 2 and to the cost of servicing the $250,000 facility. With fixed costs of $315,000 a year and a 5.4% rejection rate to fix, keeping $350,000 inside the business protects cash flow and leaves more of the $7.00 contribution per unit available for operating the magnetic separators.

Point 2: An overdraft is repayable on demand, so relying more heavily on one would leave Tomas Minegate's private limited company exposed if the bank withdrew the facility while the $600,000 plant was only part-installed. Retained profit is permanent funding and gives MNG freedom to invest at its own pace. That stability matters when 71% of surveyed solar-glass buyers require purity certificates and the plant must reach consistent quality before those customers will place larger orders, especially as the overdraft carries interest while the $350,000 of retained profit does not.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over an overdraft identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis of MNG's $350,000 retained profit, overdraft and quality demands.

questions.question_text: MNG is promoting its low-iron silica sand to solar-glass makers. Consider technical brochures at industry exhibitions, a dedicated sales team, or sponsored research with a glass institute. Which should MNG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Technical brochures at exhibitions: Printed purity data would reach many solar-glass buyers in one place and suit a technical product where 71% of the 540 surveyed buyers require purity certificates. It is relatively cheap for a 50-employee plant. Nevertheless, exhibitions are occasional, stand costs and staff time add up, and many visitors are not serious buyers; brochures alone cannot demonstrate that the new magnetic-separation plant consistently meets the 5.4% rejection target.

Dedicated sales team: A salesperson can visit solar-glass makers, explain the separation process, negotiate contracts and handle the 12 monthly quality complaints personally. This builds long-term relationships and can justify the $0.70 premium that 59% of buyers might accept. The drawback is cost: salaries and travel add to fixed costs near $315,000 a year, and a new salesperson needs technical training during a period when there is already a skills gap with the separators.

Sponsored research with a glass institute: Joint research would test MNG's sand under real glass-making conditions and produce independent evidence of purity, which is powerful for the 71% requiring certificates. It could also improve the product and reduce the 5.4% rejection rate. It is slow, however, and a small private limited company spending $600,000 on plant may struggle to fund a long research programme with immediate returns uncertain.

Recommendation: MNG should choose a dedicated sales team, with technical brochures used as support. Sales effort is not rejected outright, but it must be rather small at first because of the cost; it wins over brochures because it converts the 59% premium segment and handles complaints, and it wins over sponsored research because it produces nearer-term orders. Brochures are rejected as passive and research as too slow and expensive while the $600,000 plant needs steady demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Names the options with little reference to MNG's buyers or product.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in MNG's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends one with explicit reasons for rejecting the alternatives.

questions.question_text: MNG has a skills gap and a 5.4% rejection rate. Explain two benefits for MNG of using autocratic leadership during the commissioning of its new magnetic separators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Tomas Minegate make swift, firm decisions about separator settings and safety while the new $600,000 plant is commissioned, which matters when a skills gap means 12 of the 50 operators lack experience. Clear instructions from the top reduce the chance that inconsistent settings cause the 5.4% impurity-related rejection rate to rise, and the hierarchical structure makes it obvious who gives the orders and who carries them out.

Point 2: Tight control also helps impose uniform quality checks, so the 18,750 units processed each quarter are tested the same way and the 29 to 12 fall in monthly complaints can continue. For a private limited company relying on 71% of buyers who require purity certificates, consistent procedures protect the $350,000 retained profit invested in the plant. Decisions are fast, which suits a technical commissioning period, though the style may need to soften later if MNG wants operators to suggest improvements to the separation process.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for analysis applied to MNG's skills gap, rejection rate, structure and certificates.

questions.question_text: MNG must train 12 operators on the magnetic separators. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job external courses at $1,250 per employee. Which should MNG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning at the separators teaches the exact settings and impurity checks MNG needs, costs no course fee and keeps the 12 operators contributing to the 18,750 units processed each quarter. Immediate feedback from experienced staff can reduce the 5.4% rejection rate quickly and suits a hierarchical structure where supervisors control standards. Its weaknesses are that trainers are taken from their own work, that mistakes made during practice can create rejected sand, and that no external certificate is produced for the 71% of buyers who require purity certificates.

Off-the-job external courses: At $1,250 per employee, training all 12 operators costs $15,000, only a small part of the $600,000 investment, and an external provider can give a qualification and up-to-date theory on magnetic separation. This improves the skills base and strengthens MNG's claim to consistent purity. The problem is that 12 of 50 workers are away from the plant, risking the 18,750-unit quarterly output and potentially pushing complaints back toward 29 a month; generic course content may also need site-specific follow-up before it changes practice.

Decision: MNG should choose on-the-job training first and fund external courses for a smaller group of supervisors afterwards. On-the-job training wins on cost, relevance and uninterrupted output, and is only rejected as a complete solution because it lacks certification. Full off-the-job training for all 12 is rejected now because losing nearly a quarter of the workforce and spending $15,000 while a skills gap and 5.4% rejection rate already exist would disrupt the commissioning of the separators.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to MNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both methods using MNG's figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Fully evaluates both methods in MNG's context and reaches a justified decision that rejects the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MNG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $315,000 ÷ ($17.00 − $10.00) = $315,000 ÷ $7.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $17.00 − $10.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MNG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 75,000 units: the margin of safety is 30,000 units, so MNG can see how far solar-glass orders might fall before the $600,000 separation plant fails to cover its $315,000 fixed costs.
2. Use the $7.00 contribution per unit to test the survey result that 59% of buyers would pay $0.70 more: a price of $17.70 would raise contribution to $7.70, worth 75,000 × $0.70 = $52,500 a year if achieved on all units.
3. Check funding capacity: at 75,000 units total contribution is 75,000 × $7.00 = $525,000, leaving $210,000 after fixed costs to pay the $26,000 interest and reduce the $250,000 overdraft.
4. Benchmark costs with average total cost of $14.20 ($315,000 ÷ 75,000 + $10.00) and labour productivity of 75,000 ÷ 50 = 1,500 units per worker, so managers can tell whether the 5.4% rejection rate or the skills gap is raising cost per unit above that level.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 30,000-unit margin of safety; $0.70 premium worth $52,500; total contribution of $525,000 for overdraft planning; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.20 with 1,500 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each of four valid applied uses in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MNG's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MNG's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 37.5%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 14.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,120,000 revenue − $700,000 cost of sales = $420,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,350,000 − $810,000 = $540,000. For 2024, $420,000 ÷ $1,120,000 = 0.375; $112,000 operating profit ÷ $1,120,000 = 0.100; $112,000 ÷ $800,000 capital employed = 0.140. For 2025, $540,000 ÷ $1,350,000 = 0.400; $162,000 ÷ $1,350,000 = 0.120; $162,000 ÷ $900,000 = 0.180.

Evaluation: Revenue increased by ($1,350,000 − $1,120,000) ÷ $1,120,000 = 20.5%, while cost of sales rose by $110,000, so gross profit grew from $420,000 to $540,000. The improvement in gross margin is consistent with the survey finding that 59% of buyers would pay $0.70 more for low-iron sand. Operating profit rose from $112,000 to $162,000, faster than revenue, which suggests the $315,000 fixed costs were absorbed better even though the plant still rejects 5.4% of output. ROCE improved strongly from 14.0% to 18.0% despite capital employed rising from $800,000 to $900,000, so the additional investment in magnetic separation is earning more, not just adding assets. Interest payable rose from $22,000 to $26,000 because of the $250,000 overdraft, but this is small relative to the growth in operating profit.

Conclusion: MNG's profitability has improved. Gross margin rose from 37.5% to 40.0%, operating margin from 10.0% to 12.0% and ROCE from 14.0% to 18.0%, and the return on capital increased while the asset base grew. The only caution is the interest charge on the overdraft, but the $600,000 separation plant is currently adding value rather than diluting returns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Quotes figures from Appendix 2 without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three ratios for both years and describes the trend with some MNG context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years plus evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest with a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MNG of adding purity certification to its low-iron silica sand.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 540 solar-glass buyers found that 71% require purity certificates, so holding one lets MNG meet an existing procurement condition and strengthens its case for the $0.70 premium that 59% would pay. Certification supports the $17.00 selling price and the $7.00 contribution per unit, helps justify the $600,000 magnetic-separation investment and gives buyers confidence while the rejection rate is being reduced from 5.4%.

Disadvantage: Obtaining and maintaining certification takes testing, records and fees that could raise the $10.00 variable cost or the $315,000 fixed costs, and the 12.8% rise in energy and separation-medium costs will make consistent purity harder to afford. If the new separators cannot hold the 5.4% rejection rate, certification could be withdrawn, leaving MNG with extra costs but none of the premium from the 59% of buyers, and with the 29 monthly complaints at risk of returning. The private limited company would then have spent $600,000 on a plant that cannot satisfy the 71% of certified buyers it was built to serve.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development using the survey, price, costs and rejection data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.10%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 12.8% rise in energy and separation-medium costs will affect MNG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.10%): The bulletin links this directly to short-term borrowing such as overdrafts. If MNG's $250,000 facility tracks the 0.60 percentage point increase, the extra cost is 0.006 × $250,000 = $1,500 a year, which is minor beside fixed costs of $315,000 and operating profit of $162,000. The $350,000 of retained profit invested in the plant already limits the amount exposed, and MNG can negotiate a lower facility or repay it faster, so this change is the smallest of the three.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, from $13.10 to $14.00 an hour): With a workforce of 50, higher wages for eligible plant staff raise costs and are unavoidable. No hours worked or individual pay rates appear in the insert, so any annual wage total would be invented and is not given. The supported comparison is labour productivity of 75,000 units ÷ 50 workers = 1,500 units per worker. If the skills gap is closed and rejection stays around 5.4%, the additional wage cost is spread over 1,500 units each; if output falls, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution is reduced. The effect is genuine but manageable through training and productivity.

Input-cost inflation (12.8% on energy and separation media): The insert states variable cost of $10.00 per unit but gives no breakdown, so an honest upper bound treats it all as exposed: 12.8% × $10.00 = $1.28 per unit, and across 75,000 units that is $96,000 a year (75,000 × $1.28). Even a smaller exposed share would materially cut the $7.00 contribution, and energy is essential to the magnetic separators that underpin the 71% certificate requirement. The $0.70 premium can recover only a fraction of that amount.

Conclusion: The 12.8% rise in energy and separation-medium costs will have the greatest impact. It affects all 75,000 units, can remove about $96,000 of contribution on the stated bound and threatens the quality that wins certified buyers. The interest rise costs only $1,500 a year on the $250,000 facility, and the wage rise can be offset by maintaining 1,500 units per worker, so neither is as severe or as broad as input-cost inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Lists the three changes with limited application to MNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses at least two changes using MNG's figures with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context with insert-derived arithmetic and a justified greatest-impact conclusion.
